title: How Should a Game Begin? | Opening Design Through Zelda: Breath of the Wild

scenes.title: What should the opening promise?
lines: Think of the moment you leave the shrine in Breath of the Wild. You take in the vast landscape, then move into it yourself. Admiring a beautiful backdrop is different from expecting to actually go there.
Today, let's look at what players should see when a game begins. Not the placement of menu buttons, but the design of the first scene they can control.
That first scene makes a promise about the experience ahead. In an exploration game, it might be somewhere you want to visit. In a mystery, it might be a clue you want to investigate.
But when explanations line up before that promise, you arrive for an adventure and get employee orientation instead. What matters is not whether you explain things, but what players experience first.

Let's compare two ways to open the same scene. One explains the setting and controls in order. The other first shows the character and a nearby destination. We are comparing opening priorities, not features.
Either way, players should recognize what they can expect from the game. Before decorating the first screen, decide what you want them to feel there.

scenes.title: Who am I, and where should I go?
lines: Let's go back inside the Shrine of Resurrection. Link wakes up, obtains the Sheikah Slate, and opens the way outside. Voice guidance and control instructions appear here too.
Breath of the Wild is not a game that explains nothing. What we are examining is how it presents an immediate action, even in an unfamiliar space.
In the first controllable scene, players need to read the relationship between their character and the surroundings. They first need to know where they are and what looks worth approaching.

You can move toward a nearby object without knowing the world's history. Separating an understanding of the setting from an understanding of the first action reduces what the opening demands all at once.

Our comparison keeps the character, exit, and interactive object the same and changes only the framing. We contrast an unclear relationship with a composition that leads the eye from character to object to exit.
Adding more arrows is not the only way to guide someone. Can the positions within the camera frame suggest the next action? That is a design question for the first scene.

scenes.title: What should the camera show first?
lines: As you explore the Great Plateau, distant terrain or buildings can become your next point of interest. Before deciding where to walk, notice what catches your eye.
Breath of the Wild also has quest guidance. Separately from that guidance, let's examine how something in the landscape can become a destination you want to reach yourself.
A wide view does not always make direction clear. When everything receives similar emphasis, deciding where to look first can become difficult.
Size, contrast, and surrounding empty space can establish an order of attention. Instead of revealing the entire route, choose what will first catch the player's eye.
With the same terrain layout, compare a view where several objects compete for attention with one that distinguishes a first point of interest. We are not adding destinations or changing the map.
If everything looks important, the whole screen is raising its hand at once. Designing the first scene also means deciding what not to emphasize.

scenes.title: What should players do first?
lines: Let's look at noticing and picking up a nearby item on the Plateau. Without starting a grand battle, a small experience emerges: looking around and finding something.
We are interested less in the item feature itself than in this action's role in the opening. It can suggest that this is a world where looking around is welcome.
The first action is more than a button check. It is a chance to communicate through play whether this is a game about observing, avoiding danger, or making choices.
Demanding several actions at once can obscure what the player has learned. First decide which single action you want them to experience in this scene.
Our comparison shows the same space with many feature instructions at once, then with one nearby object to investigate first. It illustrates how the scope of that first attempt changes.

A simple beginning does not mean the whole game must be simple. The deeper the game, the more reason to ask whether players must immediately be thrown in at the deep end. Think about the order of entry.

scenes.title: Show what the action changed
lines: In the shrine where you obtain Magnesis, you move metal plates to open a path. The game does not stop at telling you about a new ability. It lets you see what using it changes.
Do not watch only the moving object. Also notice how that movement connects to the route ahead.
After the first interaction, players need evidence that it worked. If pressing a button seems to change nothing, they may press it again instead of taking the next action.
Good feedback is not simply a flash of light. The relationship between an action and a change in the space should be visible, and that change should provide a reason to continue.
With the same button and door, compare an off-screen result with a framing that shows the door opening. This is about making the result readable, not writing switch code.
If a game needs the result to happen off-screen, sound or a brief camera cue can help. Keeping everything in one frame is not always the answer. The key is making cause and effect read as connected.

scenes.title: What does the first failure teach?
lines: As exploration continues on the Great Plateau, new problems such as cold appear. Players examine temperature and status, then consider responses such as clothing or food effects.
This happens later than the first controllable scene. It shows how learning that began in the opening develops into an experience when a new danger appears.
An opening does not have to be safe. Some games need a dangerous or unsettling beginning. What matters is what the player can understand after failing.
A failure whose cause you recognize and can respond to differs from being hurt for no apparent reason. Separate from difficulty, examine the visual clues that explain the danger.
For the same hazard, one version hides the cause while the other connects the danger zone to a change in status. We are not removing difficulty, but checking whether its reason is readable.
If the route back to another attempt is too long, early learning can become repetitive labor. Design both the presentation of danger and the flow back after failure.

scenes.title: When should explanations appear?
lines: Breath of the Wild includes the Old Man's guidance and dialogue, as well as a goal for leaving the Great Plateau. In ordinary progression, you complete four shrines, obtain the paraglider, and head into the next region.
So describing its opening as having no explanations or restrictions misses something important. Guidance and exploration coexist.

When choosing information for the first screen, separate what players need now from what they will need later. The problem may not be incorrect information, but too much information arriving before there is a reason to use it.
Conversely, some scenes become incomprehensible without an explanation. Instead of simply reducing instructions, ask whether they answer the player's current question.
Our comparison keeps the information unchanged and alters only its timing. We place a sequence that shows everything at the start beside one that offers relevant guidance after the first action.

In a story-driven game, the opening conversation may itself be the core experience. The distinction is not bad cutscenes versus good interaction. Ask whether what you are showing begins this game's experience.

scenes.title: Make players curious about what comes next
lines: Gliding beyond the Plateau lets you explore the world you have been seeing in a new way. Actions from the opening area carry into the adventure ahead.
When evaluating an opening, do not stop at whether its first screen looks good. Examine whether the expectation it creates carries into the next scene.
Ask three questions when designing the first scene. What should players see first? What action should they try? Why should the result make them want to continue?
Treat the advice about the first three minutes not as a timer for every game, but as a question about when the core experience begins. Rushing the presentation is not the point.

Our final comparison contrasts a beginning that stalls after the first goal with one whose result reveals another point of interest. Where you end the scene and what you leave behind can change the reason for the next action.

A game's first scene is not a manual that explains everything. It is an invitation to try. Rather than listing everything you want to teach, start by designing the experience you are inviting players into.
